definition: A horizontal structural member that spans an opening such as a door or window and carries the load of the construction above it. On a drawing it is usually shown as a heavy line across the opening, often with a note giving its material and size.

The horizontal bottom member of a window or door opening, or the lowest horizontal member of a framed wall. A window sill forms the base the window sits on and is often shown with a dimension to finished floor height.

A horizontal framing member placed across the top of an opening to transfer load to the adjacent framing. Also used for the top member of a window or door frame, and for a masonry unit laid across a wall to bond its two faces.

The widened, lowest part of a foundation that distributes the building load over a larger soil area. Shown on foundation plans as a dashed or solid outline with a size callout such as 24 in. by 12 in.
The vertical side member of a door or window frame. Jambs appear on enlarged plans and elevations as the vertical lines bounding the opening.
The underside of a building element, such as the underside of a beam, an eave overhang, or the exposed surface above a cabinet or ceiling change. Often dimensioned on reflected ceiling plans.
The vertical face between two stair treads, meaning the height a stair climbs in one step. Riser height is normally dimensioned on stair plans and checked against code limits.
The horizontal surface of a stair step that a person walks on, measured from the front of one riser to the front of the next.

Reinforcing bar: steel bars embedded in concrete to resist tension. On structural drawings, bar size, spacing, and cover are given in a reinforcement schedule, commonly abbreviated as #4 at 12 in. on center.

A thin, water-resistant material installed to direct water away from joints and penetrations, such as at roof edges, parapets, and window heads. Drawn as a thin line with an identifying leader on roof and wall sections.
The lower edge of a sloping roof that overhangs the wall below it. The eave line appears on elevations and roof plans as the outermost horizontal line at the roof edge.
The highest horizontal line formed where two opposing roof slopes meet. Shown on a roof plan as a heavy line running along the top of the roof.

A vertical framing member in a wall, typically wood or light-gauge steel, spaced at a regular interval such as 16 in. on center. Studs are shown on framing plans as short perpendicular ticks along the wall line.
A horizontal framing member that supports a floor or ceiling and transfers load to beams or bearing walls. Joist direction, size, and spacing are noted on framing plans.

The panel material fastened over framing to form a solid surface, such as plywood or oriented strand board on walls and roofs. Also called sheathing board or structural sheathing when it carries load.

A reinforced concrete beam cast at or below ground level that carries wall or column loads to isolated footings, often spanning between piers. Shown on foundation plans as a dashed line with a size callout.

A deliberate plane of weakness formed in a concrete slab or wall so that cracking occurs in a controlled location rather than randomly. Shown on slab plans as a single line with a note giving spacing.
A small opening left at the base of a masonry wall or above flashing to let trapped water drain out. Usually shown on wall sections as a short gap in the mortar joint at the base of the cavity.

The written portion of the contract documents, usually abbreviated as spec, that describes materials, workmanship, and quality requirements. On drawings, a note such as see spec section 03 30 00 refers the reader to it.
A tabular list on a drawing that gives the size, type, and quantity of repeated items such as doors, windows, finishes, or equipment. Schedules are keyed to the plan by a matching mark or tag.
A key on a drawing sheet that explains the symbols, line types, and abbreviations used on that sheet or throughout the set.

A circular or oval symbol placed on a plan or section that references a separate enlarged drawing. The number above the line is the detail number and the number below is the sheet where that detail is drawn.
A symbol showing where a cutting plane passes through the building, with arrows indicating the viewing direction. The letters or numbers identify the sheet and section drawing that results.
A drawing that shows a building or portion of it as seen from above, cut horizontally at a stated height, so that walls, openings, and fixtures appear in their true horizontal relationship.
